titre: The same file for two different inmates
accroche: Kansas, 1903: the body measurements of a new inmate match those of another man already in custody. Only their fingerprints tell them apart.
contenu_vulgarise:
Kansas, 1903. A man is admitted to the federal penitentiary at Leavenworth under the name Will West; he claims he has never been imprisoned before. The staff take his measurements, following the method devised by the Frenchman Alphonse Bertillon: length of the skull, of the ear, of the forearm, about ten readings which, combined, are supposed to single out one individual. A check of the files reveals that an inmate already in custody, William West, has almost identical measurements and looks strongly like him. Guards sent to check his cell find him asleep in his bed. So this is not an escapee who has come back under a false name. They really are two men.

## What the measurements could not tell apart

The penitentiary staff cannot tell the two Bertillon files apart. They then take the fingerprints of both men, a method still new in the United States: the comparison distinguishes them without the slightest ambiguity. The U.S. Department of Justice reference file notes, moreover, that many people share close anthropometric measurements, which makes Bertillonage vulnerable to this kind of confusion, whereas two sets of fingerprints never resemble each other that closely. The episode becomes a weighty argument for abandoning Bertillonage, and Leavenworth begins the systematic recording of the fingerprints of all its inmates on October 19, 1904, under the direction of inspector John Kenneth Ferrier, trained at Scotland Yard, and Major M. W. McClaughry. In 1924, the nascent Federal Bureau of Investigation merges this file with that of another agency to create the first national fingerprint database in the United States, with 810,000 fingerprint cards at the start.

## A story less certain than its legend

The anecdote has fed decades of textbooks on the birth of forensic science. Yet it is less well established than it is told. The U.S. Department of Justice reference file itself calls the episode “somewhat sensationalized,” and acknowledges that the usual account omits details from the record unearthed since by researchers. The link between the two men, in particular, remains uncertain: a fellow inmate would later claim to have known them as twins in their home region, but no document confirms it, and that same file now writes that their exact relationship remains unknown. The U.S. National Archives, for their part, present them without reservation as identical twins. Two American federal institutions, on the most repeated fact in the whole history of forensic identification, do not agree with each other.

carte.punch: Two inmates, almost the same body measurements, one file to tell them apart.
carte.idee: In 1903 at Leavenworth, an inmate shares almost identical anthropometric measurements with another already in custody. Only their fingerprints tell them apart. The anecdote, which became a textbook case of Bertillonage, hides a detail still in dispute: the real relationship between the two men.
carte.source_courte: The Will West and William West case, Leavenworth, 1903

quiz.question: Why is the Will West and William West case today an example to handle with caution rather than definitive proof of the decline of Bertillonage?
choix: Because the Leavenworth penitentiary stopped using fingerprints shortly after this episode
Because federal sources contradict each other on the link between the two men, and the account omits details found since
Because both inmates were eventually found not guilty of the acts they were charged with
Because Bertillon's anthropometric measurements turned out to be a fraudulent invention
quiz.explication: Bertillon was never exposed as a fraud, and fingerprints did replace his measurements at Leavenworth. But the U.S. Department of Justice reference file itself calls the episode “somewhat sensationalized,” and U.S. federal archives today contradict each other on the link between Will and William West.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do the penitentiary staff confirm that William West is not an escapee who came back under the name Will West?
choix: Guards sent to check his cell find him asleep in his bed
A visible scar clearly distinguished the two men
William West's fingerprints were already in another file
A guard recognizes his voice at roll call
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that guards sent to check William West's cell find him asleep there, which rules out an escapee come back under a false name.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What practical effect did the Will West and William West episode have at Leavenworth?
choix: It led to the outright abolition of the death penalty in this federal penitentiary
It became a weighty argument for abandoning Bertillonage, in favor of the systematic recording of fingerprints
It led to the temporary closure of the penitentiary for a complete administrative reorganization
It allowed a collective amnesty for all inmates with similar body measurements
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The episode becomes a weighty argument for abandoning Bertillonage, and Leavenworth begins the systematic recording of fingerprints on October 19, 1904.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Do the Department of Justice file and the U.S. National Archives agree on the link between Will and William West?
choix: Yes, both institutions jointly state that they were two strangers with no family relationship at all
Yes, both institutions agree in presenting them as brothers, but not as twins
The question was finally settled for good by a DNA test carried out in 2010
No: the Department of Justice says the link is unknown, the National Archives present them as identical twins
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Department of Justice file writes that their exact relationship remains unknown, whereas the National Archives present them without reservation as identical twins.
